before: Charles Fox Parham (1873-1929) was a Holiness preacher who taught divine healing and looked for a great outpouring before the Lord's return. In October 1900 he opened a small Bible school, called Bethel, in Topeka. He asked his students to study the book of Acts and to find what Scripture teaches about the baptism of the Holy Spirit. After searching the passages, the students came to a shared conclusion. In every account where the Spirit's coming is described, speaking in tongues followed.

The usual account says that on the first day of 1901 one of the students, Agnes Ozman, asked Parham to lay hands on her and pray that she might receive the Spirit. She began to speak in other tongues. In the days that followed Parham and many others at the school had a similar experience. Parham understood these to be real human languages, given by the Spirit so that missionaries could preach without years of language study.

In October 1900 he opened a small Bible school, called Bethel, in Topeka. He asked his students to study the book of Acts and to find what Scripture teaches about the baptism of the Holy Spirit. The students concluded that tongues accompanied Spirit baptism in the accounts they regarded as decisive. Acts explicitly reports tongues at Pentecost (Acts 2), in Cornelius's household (Acts 10), and at Ephesus (Acts 19); Acts 8 describes the Spirit's reception but does not explicitly mention tongues. Parham's conclusion became a defining classical Pentecostal interpretation, though Christians differ over how these passages should be read. [U3.1]

before: We should speak honestly about Parham. His idea that tongues would give missionaries foreign languages did not work in practice. Missionaries who went abroad expecting this did not receive the languages they needed, and many Pentecostals later changed their understanding. His later years were also marked by controversy. He opposed the Azusa Street meetings after visiting them, because of the mixing of races and the manner of the services, and his racial attitudes are rightly rejected by Pentecostals today. We honor Topeka for the question the students asked of Scripture, but we do not excuse Parham's failings.

before: William Joseph Seymour was born in Louisiana in 1870 to parents who had been enslaved. He became a Holiness minister, moved to the American Midwest and then to Texas. In Houston he heard of Parham's school. Because of the segregation laws of the time, he was not allowed to sit in the classroom with the white students, and he is reported to have listened from the hallway. He accepted Parham's teaching about tongues, though he had not yet spoken in tongues himself.

before: The group moved to a plain, run-down building at 312 Azusa Street, which had once been a church and had been used as a stable and warehouse. There the Azusa Street Mission began in April 1906. Meetings continued day after day for about three years. People of many backgrounds came: African American, white, Latino and others. Observers wrote that people prayed, sang, testified, were healed and were baptized in the Spirit with tongues. The services were not tightly planned. Seymour led with humility, and he insisted that the work belonged to God. A Los Angeles newspaper mocked the meetings, which only drew more attention.

before: In September 1906 the mission began to publish a paper called *The Apostolic Faith*. We described this source in Unit 1. It printed testimonies, reports of meetings, and letters from many places, and it was mailed to readers in many parts of the world. It also taught what the mission believed: salvation, sanctification, the baptism of the Spirit, divine healing, and the Lord's soon return. Historians such as Cecil M. Robeck Jr. have used it, together with other records, to study the mission carefully.

The message spread quickly. Visitors came to Azusa Street, received what they sought, and carried it home. G. B. Cashwell, a Holiness preacher from North Carolina, went to Los Angeles in late 1906 and returned to hold meetings in Dunn, North Carolina, from which the message spread through the Holiness churches of the American South. Thomas Ball Barratt, a Methodist minister in Norway, received the experience in New York in 1906 and took it to Norway and then to other parts of Europe. Charles H. Mason, who will appear again in Unit 4, was among those who traveled to Azusa Street. Missionaries went out to many nations. Not all were wise in their preparation, but many were faithful.

before: **Wales (1904-1905).** In the autumn of 1904 a revival began in Wales, associated with the young preacher Evan Roberts, who came from a mining family. It was marked by prayer, congregational singing, confession of sin and many conversions. The Welsh revival was not Pentecostal in the sense of teaching tongues as the sign of Spirit baptism. But reports of it traveled by letter and newspaper to many countries. In Los Angeles, Frank Bartleman, a Holiness preacher, read these reports and urged believers to pray for the same outpouring in their city. Wales stirred the hunger that Azusa Street later met.

**Mukti, India (1905).** Pandita Ramabai (1858-1922) was an Indian Christian scholar and reformer who cared for widows, orphans and famine victims at the Mukti mission near Pune. In 1905 the mission experienced a revival marked by prayer, confession of sin and spiritual gifts. The American missionary Minnie Abrams, who worked at Mukti, wrote about it in *The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire* (1906). The revival was led by an Indian woman and took place before Azusa Street. It shows that the Spirit did not wait for one American city.

**Chile (1909).** Willis Hoover was an American Methodist missionary and the pastor of a Methodist church in Valparaiso. In 1909 a revival began in his congregation, with prayer, healing and tongues. Reports from other places, including Mukti, had reached the church. Methodist authorities did not accept the revival, and in 1910 Hoover and many of his congregation left to form a new church, the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal. It was led by Chileans and grew into a large national church. We will return to it in Unit 6.
after: **Wales (1904-1905).** In the autumn of 1904 a revival began in Wales, associated with the young preacher Evan Roberts, who came from a mining family. It was marked by prayer, congregational singing, confession of sin and many conversions. The Welsh revival was not a classical Pentecostal movement teaching tongues as the initial evidence of Spirit baptism. Historians differ over how directly to connect it with Pentecostalism; it is best described here as a revival that influenced some early Pentecostal prayer and expectations. Reports of it traveled by letter and newspaper to many countries. Frank Bartleman later wrote that Welsh revival reports influenced his own prayers for revival in Los Angeles. This documents an influence on one early Pentecostal observer; historians differ over how directly Wales shaped the Azusa revival or the formation of classical Pentecostalism. [U3.8]

**Mukti, India (1905).** Pandita Ramabai (1858-1922) was an Indian Christian scholar and reformer who cared for widows, orphans and famine victims at the Mukti mission near Pune. In 1905 the mission experienced a revival marked by prayer, confession of sin and spiritual gifts. The American missionary Minnie Abrams, who worked at Mukti, wrote about it in *The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire* (1906). The revival was led by an Indian woman and took place before Azusa Street. It shows that the Spirit did not wait for one American city. [U3.9]

**Chile (1909–1910).** Willis Hoover was an American Methodist missionary and pastor in Valparaiso. A revival took shape among Methodists in 1909. The Chilean National Library dates the founding of the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal to September 12, 1909, while some summaries emphasize the 1910 separation from Methodist oversight. These dates refer to related stages, so this course preserves both rather than assigning one uncontested founding date. The church was led by Chileans and became a major national body. We return to it in Unit 6. [U3.10]

3. Why should the Welsh revival be distinguished from classical Pentecostalism even while discussing its influence?
